newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cr. Lyonnais investment certificates soar.
newsitem.headline: Cr. Lyonnais investment certificates soar.

text.p: Investors bought holdings in state-controlled Credit Lyonnais on Friday, driving its investment certificates up 16 percent, on hopes the government was close to agreeing a new rescue plan for the bank.
The certificates, which make up 21 percent of the capital but carry no voting rights soared 17.9 francs ($3.52) to 130.9 francs.

Credit Lyonnais, whose downfall marked one of the worst banking scandals in French history, and the state have been in talks for months about how to amend last year's state bailout which has proved to be a millstone around the bank's neck.
Reports say under the new scheme, most of the heavy costs imposed on the bank as part of an effort to make it bear some of the pain for its reckless past would likely be waived.

The talks are said to centre on cancelling a 119 billion franc loan it was forced to make at below market rates to help finance its rescue after posting losses of 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994 as a result of an ill-judged expansion spree.
Analysts say the terms of the loan could push it into a three billion franc loss for the year and are estimating a loss of between one billion and 1.5 billion francs for the half year.
Without the loan, "it would probably be making a modest profit or at least be at breakeven," said one analyst.
The bank, struggling in France's depressed banking climate, posted a 13 million franc profit last year.

But although changing the rescue would "take the pressure off in the near term, it doesn't answer the underlying problems which are ones of strategy and underlying profitability," said banking analyst Jennifer Oliver Martin of Morgan Stanley.
The government and the bank have been in a race against time to come up with new salvage terms before the half-year results on September 26.
The bank said its chairman Jean Peyrelevade was still at his desk and had not resigned after a report surfaced Thursday he had threatened to quit on Friday if a deal was not reached.
One source said the resignation threat was made in July when talks were deadlocked. Since then, attitudes have changed with government officials accepting the need to change the plan.
He said the new plan would likely be released at the same time as the half-year results. ($ = 5.077 French Francs)
